Threat.value: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home

Memory.value: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event

vignette:
Layla reports that the six months since the assault have felt like living in a different, more dangerous world. The event itself, a home invasion in the late afternoon, is a collection of searingly bright fragments and bewildering black voids in her memory. She remembers the splintering sound of the back door frame with perfect clarity, the smell of stale cigarette smoke on the intruder's jacket, and the terrifyingly casual way he told her she wasn't the first person this had happened to. But she cannot recall his face, nor can she piece together how she ended up on the floor by the kitchen island. This feeling of an incomplete picture haunts her; she is certain that the missing pieces hold something even more terrible, a truth her mind refuses to let her see. When a fragment of the memory does break through-usually the image of his arm reaching for her-it is accompanied by a sharp, radiating pain in her right shoulder, a phantom of the force he used to shove her down.

In the weeks that followed, Layla's sense of safety evaporated, first at home and then at work. Her own house, once a sanctuary, became a source of constant threat. She found herself unable to relax, her ears perpetually strained, listening for the subtle click of a lock or the creak of a floorboard that might signal an intruder. Her husband, Sameer, learned not to come home unannounced, as the sound of his key in the door could send her into a state of rigid panic. The television became another source of dread. Any news report about violence against women, any reminder of other victims, felt like a direct confirmation of her own vulnerability and the attacker's chilling words. She came to believe that the world was fundamentally unsafe and that she was marked by what had happened.

This pervasive sense of threat followed her to her job as a housekeeper. The large, quiet suburban homes she cleaned, once spaces of peaceful solitude, now felt like traps. She would find her mind drifting from her tasks, her attention snagged not on the dust she was supposed to be wiping, but on the unlocked patio door or the rustle of leaves outside a window. She began a constant, silent patrol of her surroundings, scanning driveways from upstairs windows and checking that all doors were bolted before she would even start her work. This hypervigilance shattered her ability to concentrate. She would forget which rooms she had cleaned, mix up cleaning solutions, and once left a client's front door unlocked all day. Her manager's patience wore thin. The final straw came when the manager, frustrated with a missed task, cornered her in a hallway and said sharply, "Layla, you will go back and do the master bathroom right now." The feeling of being trapped, of being forced to do something against her will, was so overwhelming that she dropped her supplies, walked out, and never went back.

The loss of her job has strained her marriage and deepened her isolation. Sameer's attempts to comfort her often backfire. His raised voice while watching a football match can make her flinch and retreat to the bedroom. She feels a chasm growing between them, built from his confusion and her inability to explain the terror that governs her every moment. Layla sought therapy after a particularly bad night when, woken by a nightmare, she began frantically checking the windows. Sameer tried to gently guide her back to bed, and she screamed at him not to touch her. The look of shock and hurt on his face made her realize she could not navigate this alone. She is terrified that she is broken beyond repair, but she holds onto a fragile hope of one day feeling calm in her own home again, of not having to constantly stand guard against a danger that might only exist in her mind.
